questions.question: In DDIA terms, reliability mainly means:
options: The UI always uses the same shade of blue on every button forever.
The system continues to work correctly even when things go wrong.
You never deploy new features so nothing can ever break again.
Every request is rejected so the servers stay idle and “stable.”
questions.explanation: What it means for a service to be reliable - namely, continuing to work correctly, even when things go wrong

reference.book: Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann
reference.excerpt: These are your functional requirements. In addition, you probably have nonfunctional requirements: for example, the app should be fast, reliable, secure, legally compliant, and easy to maintain.

books.book: System Design Interview - An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
books.excerpt: Best part: this book is very technical and contains a lot of in-depth discussion about scalability, consistency, reliability, efficiency and maintainability.

questions.question: Scalability, as framed in DDIA, is about:
options: Buying one infinitely powerful machine so you never rethink architecture.
Having efficient ways to add computing capacity as load on the system grows.
Deleting all indexes so writes are always fast regardless of read patterns.
Turning off monitoring so you do not notice when load increases.
questions.explanation: Allowing a system to be scalable by having efficient ways of adding computing capacity as the load on the system grows

reference.book: Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann
reference.excerpt: Scalability is not a one-dimensional label - it is meaningless to say “X is scalable” or “Y doesn’t scale.” Rather, discussing scalability means considering questions like these: If the system grows in a particular way, what are our options for coping with the growth?

questions.question: DDIA notes that an architecture appropriate for one load level:
options: Always handles 10× load with zero changes if the logo is redesigned.
Is unlikely to cope with 10× that load - rethink on each order-of-magnitude growth.
Must be microservices from day one even with ten users.
Can ignore databases entirely once traffic doubles once.
questions.explanation: an architecture that is appropriate for one level of load is unlikely to cope with 10 times that load

reference.book: Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann
reference.excerpt: Even when the load is reduced again, such a system may remain in an overloaded state until it is rebooted or otherwise reset.

questions.question: Nonfunctional requirements such as speed and reliability:
options: Can be ignored because only button labels matter to users.
Are as important as functionality - a slow or unreliable app is barely usable.
Only apply to mainframe systems from the 1970s and never web apps.
Are automatically satisfied by any framework with a popular name.
questions.explanation: an app that is unbearably slow or unreliable might as well not exist

reference.book: Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann
reference.excerpt: These requirements might not be explicitly written down, because they may seem somewhat obvious, but they are just as important as the app’s functionality; an app that is unbearably slow or unreliable might as well not exist.

questions.question: True or false: Maintainability is about making the system easier to keep evolving over the long term.
questions.explanation: Making it easier to maintain a system in the long term

reference.book: Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann

questions.question: When discussing scalability in an interview, you should first clarify:
options: Only the color of the status page banner during an outage.
Load parameters (QPS, users, data size, read/write mix) before proposing scale-out.
That vertical scaling forever is always cheaper than any other option.
That caching is illegal in all production systems worldwide.
questions.explanation: back-of-the-envelope calculations… to get a good feel for which designs will meet your requirements

questions.question: Fault tolerance / high availability typically involves:
options: Running a single server with no backups so failures are simple.
Using multiple machines for redundancy so another can take over on failure.
Never writing logs because logs cause all outages.
Blocking all users permanently to keep error rates at zero.
questions.explanation: you can use multiple machines to give you redundancy. When one fails, another one can take over

reference.book: Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann
reference.excerpt: Fault tolerance/high availability If your application needs to continue working even if one machine (or several machines, or the network, or an entire datacenter) goes down, you can use multiple machines to give you redundancy.
